Tuesday.
Counted today: I checked the news eleven times, refilled my water bottle six times, reorganised my desktop folders, and read half an article about octopuses. Actual work: maybe ninety minutes.
It's not that there's too much. There's too little. Same reconciliation sheets I've done for two years. I could do them half asleep, and mostly I do.
I feel guilty about it all day. Uday, at the next desk, is always busy and slightly stressed. I'm neither.
Tonight I tried to work out what the boredom is asking for. It isn't rest. I sleep fine. It isn't fun, exactly. I think it's difficulty. Something I can't already do.
Tomorrow I'll ask my manager if I can help with the new vendor audit. It's messy and nobody wants it. That might be exactly why I do.
— Jaya

The sub-post office in Nanjangud opened at nine, and by eleven Varun had nothing left to do. He sold four stamps, weighed two parcels, and filed the savings slips. Then the long, hot afternoon.
He rearranged the rubber stamps by colour. He read the old notice board. He checked his phone until the screen blurred. Each time the postmaster passed, Varun felt a prick of guilt and pretended to check a ledger.

“I'm fine.”
“You're bored. You were the one who fixed the counter computer last year. Why don't you ask to set up the online tracking the district office keeps talking about?”
Varun thought about it. It would be hard. He'd have to learn it.
For the first time that afternoon, he felt interested instead of guilty.

When I was nine, in Shillong, my father brought home a metal building set from a fair: little nuts and bolts and strips with holes. My brothers lost interest in a day. I didn't.
I built a bridge first. Then a windmill that actually turned. I remember sitting on the verandah floor, the light moving across it, and my mother calling me for lunch, then for tea. I didn't hear either time.
Some bolts wouldn't fit. I'd get so cross. Then I'd try another way, and it would click, and I'd feel a happiness that went all the way through me.

passage:
In my first year teaching at the polytechnic, I'm Rafiq, and I met Seema, a second-year electrical student who had stopped trying.
She sat with her textbook closed. In the lab she let her partners do everything. When I asked her about a circuit, she said, “I can't do this, Sir. I've failed two practicals. It doesn't matter what I do.”
But in her first-year file I found a project she'd built: a small solar lamp. It worked. She was capable. She'd just lost the belief that her effort mattered.
So I gave her one simple job: wire a single bulb to a switch. She did it in ten minutes. The bulb lit. I just said, “Good. Next.”
The next week, two bulbs in series. Then a fan regulator.
By the end of term, she was helping her partners. The belief came back slowly, the way a bulb warms up.

qa.q: What project had Seema built in first year?
qa.a: She had built a small solar lamp that worked.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel on finding the solar-lamp project?
qa.a: Rafiq felt encouraged and more determined, seeing that Seema was capable and had only lost belief in her effort.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq's simple tasks work?
qa.a: Each small task was one Seema could succeed at, and the growing successes slowly broke her belief that effort was useless.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when the first bulb lit?
qa.a: Seema probably felt a flicker of surprise and relief, a first sign her effort could work.

grounding: The teacher's account shows someone seeing a capable student give up and assigning small tasks she can succeed at, rebuilding belief.

At some point last year, I stopped asking for things at home. I'm Naveen. I live with my brother's family, and I used to ask for small things: a quiet hour on Sundays, help with the electricity bill, a turn choosing the TV.
Every request was ignored or waved off. So I stopped.
I didn't notice the change at first. I just felt… nothing much. I ate, went to work, came home, lay on my bed. My friend Nikita said I talked like I was underwater.
She kept asking questions until I told her about the months of flatness. She said, “That's been going on a long time. I think you should talk to someone qualified.” I said I'd think about it.
She sent me the number of a counsellor that night. I booked an appointment the next day. I don't know yet what will change. But asking for this one thing felt like the first real choice I'd made in months.

Bhupen has worked on this shift for two years. He used to raise things often: a broken forklift light, a request for a day shift, a safety ramp at bay 4. None were acted on by the previous management.
Since I took over in March, I have noticed he no longer asks for anything. When I asked what would make the shift easier, he said, “Nothing, Sir. Doesn't matter.” His colleague Yogesh told me Bhupen “used to joke all the time” and now barely talks.
He seemed flat and far away. I was concerned.
What I did next: the same week I fixed the forklift light and the bay 4 ramp, and told him plainly that these were his requests. I also told him about our employee counselling service, which is confidential, and said if his mood has been heavy for a while, talking to someone could help. He took the card. I will check in with him next Friday.

In the village near Sangli, it was the first week of the rains. Zainab, eight, asked her mother Uma for a patch of the courtyard.
“For what?”
“To plant.”
Uma gave her a corner by the wall and a handful of okra seeds. “You decide where.”
Zainab chose carefully. She poked five holes with her finger, dropped in the seeds, patted the mud and watered them every evening from a steel lota.
For six days, nothing. She sat by the patch and sulked.
On the seventh morning, she screamed so loud the neighbour's hen ran. Three tiny green loops had pushed up out of the soil.
“Ammi! Mine! I planted them!”
From then on she checked them before brushing her teeth. When one drooped in the sun, she moved a broken pot to shade it. It stood up by evening.

qa.q: How many seeds did Zainab plant?
qa.a: She planted five okra seeds.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel on the seventh morning?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and proud, screaming with joy because the plants were hers.

qa.q: What did Uma do that helped Zainab learn that her actions matter?
qa.a: She let Zainab decide where to plant and care for them herself, so the sprouts were clear evidence of Zainab's own effort.

qa.q: How might Uma feel watching Zainab shade the drooping plant?
qa.a: Uma probably feels proud and touched, seeing her daughter take care of something she started.

grounding: The passage shows a child deciding where to plant seeds, caring for them and seeing them grow, learning that her actions change things.

In a small flat in Amman, the toy truck Yosef loved had lost a wheel. He brought it to his big sister Nour, holding it out.
“Fix it?”
Nour looked at it. “You fix it. I'll hold the torch.”
Yosef, nine, frowned. He found the wheel under the sofa. He tried pushing it on. It fell off. He tried again. It fell off. He looked at the axle and saw it was bent.
“Can I use your ruler?”
He pressed the axle straight against the ruler, slowly, carefully. Then he pushed the wheel on.
It stayed. He rolled the truck across the tiles, and it went straight.
Yosef looked at the truck, then at his hands. “I did that.”
“You did,” said Nour.
The next week, when the door handle of his cupboard came loose, he went looking for a screwdriver himself.

qa.a: He felt proud and a bit amazed, looking at his hands and saying “I did that.”

passage:
After Lalremsiami's father lost his job in March, the flat in Aizawl went quiet in a heavy way. Her parents talked in low voices. Lalremsiami, fifteen, felt like the ground had gone soft under her.
She stopped doing homework. What was the point, if everything was falling apart?
The school counsellor, Mr Darshan, didn't give her advice. He gave her a sheet of paper with a line down the middle. “Left side: things you can influence. Right side: things you can't.”
Right side came fast: Papa's job. Money. Whether we move.
Left side was slower: Study for one hour after school. Help Mama with dinner. Talk to Mr Darshan on Thursdays. Tell Papa I love him.
She stuck the sheet inside her cupboard. That night she did one hour of history. It didn't fix anything. But for an hour, she felt a little less helpless.

qa.q: What was on the right side of Lalremsiami's list first?
qa.a: Papa's job, money and whether they move.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel after doing an hour of history that night?
qa.a: She felt a little less helpless, even though nothing at home was fixed.

qa.q: Why did the two-column list help?
qa.a: It separated what she could influence from what she couldn't, and acting on the first list gave her back some sense of power.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami's father feel if she tells him she loves him?
qa.a: He would likely feel touched and comforted during a hard time.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager in a hard family situation listing what she can influence and acting on it, restoring a sense of power.

The month my parents told us they were separating, I felt like I was sitting in a car with no brakes. I'm Tanvir, fifteen, and I couldn't sleep or study.
My older sister Simran found me one night on the stairs. She didn't say “it'll be fine.” She said, “Let's make two lists.”
The first list, things I couldn't change: whether they separate, where Papa lives, what they argue about.
The second, things I could: going to bed by eleven, finishing my science project, talking to the school counsellor, calling Simran when it got bad, playing football on Saturdays.
I pinned the second list above my desk. The first list I folded and put in a drawer.
It didn't make the separation hurt less. But it gave my hands something to do, and my head a place to stand.
